Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette: Jamila sat quietly in her armchair, her eyes fixed on a faded photograph of her late husband and their children. It had been two years since her granddaughter's life-threatening illness, a grueling ordeal that left Jamila feeling shattered and forever changed. The memories of those agonizing days still lingered, refusing to be extinguished by the passage of time. As she recalled the hospital room where her granddaughter lay helpless, connected to an array of medical equipment, Jamila was suddenly overcome with emotion. Her eyes welled up, and her breath caught in her throat. The sterile smell wafting from the antiseptic wipes used to clean her granddaughter's skin had become forever linked to that traumatic experience. Even now, when she walked past a hospital or caught a whiff of something similar, Jamila felt like she was right back there - powerless and consumed by fear. At first, Jamila tried to suppress these memories, pushing them aside with all her might. But they refused to be contained, forcing their way into her mind at the most inopportune moments. Sometimes, while watching TV or cooking dinner, a snippet of conversation about someone losing a loved one would transport her back to that excruciating time. Other times, the mere sight of medical equipment - needles, drips, and monitors - sent shivers down her spine. Jamila's attempts at thought suppression had been valiant but ultimately unsuccessful. The memories lingered, casting a dark shadow over every aspect of her life. As a social worker, she'd always prided herself on being available for others, offering comfort and support whenever needed. But now, Jamila found it increasingly difficult to venture out into public spaces. Even visiting friends or going grocery shopping became daunting tasks. "What if I see someone in distress?" she'd think to herself. "What if I'm reminded of the hospital again?" She began avoiding hospitals altogether - no more volunteering at local health fairs, no more visits to sick friends. Jamila even stopped attending medical appointments for her own chronic condition, citing trivial excuses and risking further complications. As these avoidance behaviors took hold, Jamila's daily life shrunk dramatically. Her loved ones expressed concern about her increasingly reclusive nature, but she couldn't explain the paralyzing fear that gripped her whenever she contemplated stepping outside. Even conversations with friends became strained, as they struggled to discuss their own family losses without inadvertently triggering Jamila's memories. Jamila had come to believe that she'd acted in ways that went against who she was - strong and resilient - during those fateful days. The realization left an indelible mark on her self-perception. "I should have been more present," she'd think, "more supportive for my granddaughter." This notion of permanent damage had taken hold, convincing Jamila that a part of her had been irreparably broken. At night, as the darkness settled around her, Jamila would lie awake, consumed by an overwhelming sense of grief. Tears streamed down her face as she remembered those terrible days and the memories she'd tried so hard to suppress. The pain still lingered - an open wound that refused to heal. "What if I had done something differently?" she'd think. "Would things have turned out better?" One evening, after a particularly distressing episode of memory recall, Jamila realized she couldn't continue living like this. Her granddaughter was recovering well now, but the emotional toll on Jamila remained unaddressed. She knew it was time to seek help - not just for her own sake but also to prove to herself that even in the darkest moments, healing and growth were possible. The phone number of a local therapist lay scribbled on a piece of paper beside her chair, left there by an insistent friend. With trembling hands, Jamila picked up the receiver and dialed the number - her voice barely above a whisper as she took that first tentative step toward confronting the memories that had haunted her for so long.
